title: Durga, the Boat Across
hookLine: night two: the buffalo demon has fallen, and the gods praise the warrior goddess as a boat
carry: durga is the boat across samsara's ocean
last: NIGHT ONE: A SEAT FOR HER.

cards: The battlefield has gone quiet. Mahisha, the buffalo demon who drove the gods out of heaven, lies dead, and the goddess who killed him is still standing there, weapons in all her hands.
The gods, led by Indra, step forward to sing to her. You'd expect them to praise her as a sword, or a fortress. Partway through, they call her something else.

teach.h: THE GODS SING AFTER THE VICTORY.
teach.b: It's in the fourth chapter of the Devi Mahatmya, and the line plays on her name. In paraphrase: you are Durga, the boat across the hard-to-cross ocean of worldly life.
Her name, Durga, sits right beside durga, hard to cross, the word the gods use for that ocean. The one named for what's hard to get through is the boat that gets people through it.
And that ocean has a name in Hindu teaching: samsara, the round of birth, death and birth again, with all its worry and wanting.

Many Hindu prayers call it bhava-sagara, the ocean of becoming, and ask God to carry them across. The gods have just watched her win a war, and they don't only praise her as a weapon. They praise her as the way across.
Some readers hear her name point two ways: toward anyone who threatens her people, she's hard to get past, like a wall; toward anyone in trouble, she's the boat.
That's why so many Hindus turn to Durga when life is hardest.
Her fierceness faces outward, at what threatens; to the one who comes to her, she's refuge.

In these first nights some devotees dwell on her battles, reading the demons as anger, pride and confusion, and keep a fast or recite the chapters; others put the weight on the boat, and simply come to her temple, or her lamp, with what they can't carry.
The second night asks: what are you trying to cross alone?

how: During the first nights of Navaratri, some families keep a fast, light a lamp before an image of Durga, visit her temple, or recite chapters of the Devi Mahatmya, including the gods' hymn of praise in chapter four.

in the gods' hymn it points two ways: hard to pass, and the boat across.
in the Devi Mahatmya, the gods praise her after the buffalo demon falls

games.q: you're one of the gods. the buffalo demon has fallen and you're singing to the goddess. you want to say what her name means to you. what do you sing?
o: you are Durga, the boat across the hard ocean.
you are Durga, who should leave us alone now.
you are Durga, who needs nothing from us.
games.why: the gods' hymn plays on her name: Durga, hard to pass, is also the boat across what is hard to cross.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that feels hard to cross this week and look at it plainly. Then ask: am I trying to swim this alone? If you pray, bring it to Durga, or to God, in your own words, the way the gods did: you are the boat.
If you don't, think of one person or one practice that could carry you part of the way, and let that be enough for tonight.

wordCard.voice: Durga. Night two, in her first stretch of nights: the goddess whose name the gods set beside hard to cross, praised as the boat across samsara.

orig.note: Sanskrit durgā: the goddess's name; in the gods' hymn it sits beside durga, 'hard to cross,' and she is praised as the boat across.

carryVoice: Your line: Durga is the boat across samsara's ocean. Fierce outward, refuge inward. See you on night three.
